自查：有两组，也未必能交两次
回到拿卡后交付的规则，只改林的初始持有：林有两红一蓝，乔仍有一蓝；公共区仍为一红一蓝。林拿蓝卡，乔随后拿红卡，两人都尽可能交付。这段结束时各得多少分，林剩什么？
答案：林拿卡后有两红两蓝，但每次行动最多交一组，所以只得 3 分，剩一红一蓝。乔拿红后交出一组，也得 3 分。已交付区共两红两蓝，公共区空。林剩下的那组不会在阶段结束时自动计分，因为结束计分规则没有给它分数。
将连接处写进自己的原型
为一次完整行动写出次序：取得材料、检查条件、支付或交出、获得效果、检查结束。你的游戏未必采用这个顺序；关键是把自己的顺序明写出来。如果一个效果能再次触发，另写次数或停止条件。不要让玩家用“应该还能再做吧”替设计者补规则。
先用纸片重演一个会成功的过程，再重演一个不满足条件的过程。完整游戏仍要补更长的流程和目标，这些局部实验不能代替整局测试。
来源与范围
概念研究参考 Geoffrey Engelstein 与 Isaac Shalev 的 Building Blocks of Tabletop Game Design，第二版，CAR-06 “Drafting”与 SET-01 “Set Valuation”：取得元素的方式与组合的收益规则需要分开描述。本课的交付次序、一次一组限制和全部数字是本站设计的实验。
Kathleen Mercury 的 Prototyping 鼓励尽早用足以测试主要想法的材料做原型。本课据此采用少量纸片演示；不照搬课堂工期，也不声称这些算例已经证明学习效果。
Connect mechanisms: what happens after you acquire something?

“Drafting plus set scoring” is not yet an executable rule. When can a newly acquired item be used? Where do spent items go? How many sets may be submitted at once? This lesson specifies those connections through a Valley Post materials experiment.
Set up this experiment

This is a new original local phase. Lin and Qiao have 0 points each. Lin already holds one red address card and Qiao one blue postage card. All cards are face up. The shared supply contains one more red and one more blue. A separate delivered area starts empty; cards placed there do not return this phase. Colors are categories defined for the experiment, not actual postal requirements.

Lin acts first, then Qiao. Each must take one card still in the shared supply and add it to their own cards. They may then submit one red and one blue to the delivered area for 3 points, or decline to submit. Each action permits at most one submission. Players cannot use someone else's cards. There are no trades, replacement cards, or other effects.

The phase ends only after Qiao's action, including the submission opportunity. Remaining cards score nothing; earned points remain. We record this phase separately from the previous postal lessons and the crossing course.
Acquire first, then check for a submission
Lin takes the shared blue, now holds one red and one blue, and may submit them. Lin does so, scores 3, and has no cards left. Only the red remains in the supply.

Qiao takes that red, combining it with Qiao's blue. Qiao submits both for 3 points. The phase ends with both players on 3, no cards in their holdings or the supply, and two reds and two blues in the delivered area.

The supply became empty when Qiao took the card, but play must not end at that instant. Qiao still has a submission opportunity within that action. Treating an empty supply as an immediate end would incorrectly leave Lin on 3 and Qiao on 0.
Make a different legal choice and follow both players

Reset to the initial state. This time Lin takes the red, holds two reds without a blue, and cannot submit. Lin remains on 0. The only remaining shared card is blue. Qiao takes it, holds two blues without a red, and also cannot submit.

Both finish on 0, each retaining two cards of one color. The supply and delivered area are empty. Drafting determines who acquires which materials; the submission rule determines how those materials become points. Their connection produces the two different outcomes.
This does not establish that acquiring more is always better. Each player gains exactly one new card in either sequence. The difference is whether it forms a usable set with their existing card.
Move only the check, and the result changes

Keep the original cards and order. Change only the submission opportunity: it now happens before taking a card. A player first decides whether to submit one red and one blue, then takes a shared card. There is no check after acquisition. The one-submission limit and end after the final complete action remain.

Lin initially has only a red and cannot submit, then takes the blue. Qiao initially has only a blue and cannot submit, then takes the red. Both end holding a red and a blue, but each scores 0 because their submission opportunity has passed.
Same picks: Lin takes blue, Qiao takes red · Submit after taking · Submit before taking
Points, Lin / Qiao · 3 / 3 · 0 / 0
Lin's remaining cards · None · One red, one blue
Qiao's remaining cards · None · One red, one blue
Delivered area · Two reds, two blues · Empty

The mechanisms may retain the same names while their connection changes. “Can the new card be used in this action's submission?” gives another designer something more checkable than “the combination feels awkward.”
Check: having two sets may not permit two submissions

Return to submission after taking a card. Change only Lin's starting holdings to two reds and one blue. Qiao still has one blue; the supply still contains one red and one blue. Lin takes blue, then Qiao takes red. Both submit as much as permitted. What are their scores, and what does Lin retain?

After taking blue, Lin has two reds and two blues. The action permits only one submission, so Lin scores 3 and retains one red and one blue. Qiao submits the newly completed set for 3. The delivered area contains two reds and two blues; the supply is empty. Lin's remaining set does not automatically score when the phase ends. The end-scoring rule gives it no points.
Write the connections into your prototype

Specify a complete action's order: acquire materials, check conditions, pay or submit, gain effects, and check for the end. Your game may use another order. What matters is making yours explicit. If an effect may trigger again, specify a limit or stopping condition. Players should not have to finish the design by guessing that they can repeat it.
Use paper pieces to replay one successful sequence and one that fails the conditions. A complete game still needs its broader flow and goals; local experiments do not replace whole-game testing.
Sources and scope

Conceptual research draws on Geoffrey Engelstein and Isaac Shalev, Building Blocks of Tabletop Game Design, second edition, CAR-06, “Drafting,” and SET-01, “Set Valuation”: acquiring elements and defining a set's reward are distinct rules to specify. The submission order, once-per-action limit, and all values here are original experimental rules.

Kathleen Mercury's Prototyping encourages early prototypes with enough material to test their main ideas. This lesson uses a few paper pieces for that purpose. It does not adopt her classroom timetable or claim that these calculations establish learning effectiveness.
从题材到规则：把“先准备，才能启用”写出来
“做一款灯节游戏”给了我们场景，却还没有告诉玩家能做什么。灯、摊位和布置员都可以画出来，但哪件事必须先完成，谁为它花时间？这一类关系，才开始把题材变成可以运行的规则。
下面是一段原创的灯节布置模型。它只保留“检查过的灯才能点亮”这条关系；检查条件和四次期限都是模型设定。
先选一条值得表现的关系
两名玩家扮演布置员甲、乙，共同在开场前准备左灯和右灯。两人面对的是同一目标，不分别计分。
我们希望玩家关心准备工作，于是让检查留下一个可见标记，并让这个标记决定点灯是否允许。这样，检查就不只是故事里提到的工作。它改变了下一步能做什么。
期限让这件事有代价：花一次行动检查，就少一次行动做别的事。这里还没有决定每次检查覆盖多大范围；先看逐盏处理的一版。
第一版：逐盏检查
准备两张灯牌，两盏都未检查、未点亮；两枚检查标记和两枚亮灯标记放在旁边。所有状态公开，没有随机事件。两人可以商量，并且都能操作任意一盏灯。
依次由甲、乙、甲、乙各行动一次，全队最多四次。每次只选以下一个动作：
检查：给一盏未检查的灯放上检查标记。
点亮：给一盏已经检查、尚未点亮的灯放上亮灯标记。
等待：不改变灯的状态，但用掉本次行动。
检查标记不会过期，也不会被点灯消耗。没有移动、付款或额外动作；不能直接点亮未检查的灯。两灯一旦都亮，全队立即成功。若第四次行动结束仍未完成，全队失败，没有个人排名或平手。
一种完整过程是：
行动 · 玩家做什么 · 结束后的状态
1，甲 · 检查左灯 · 左已检查，两灯未亮
2，乙 · 点亮左灯 · 左亮，右未检查
3，甲 · 检查右灯 · 左亮，右已检查
4，乙 · 点亮右灯 · 两灯都亮，成功
每盏灯都需要一次检查和一次点亮，所以完成两盏至少要四次行动。这条过程正好用完预算。不是因为规则说“你必须按这个脚本走”，而是四项必要工作都要有人完成。
第二版：一次检查整批灯
现在只改检查动作的范围：只要还有未检查的灯，一次行动就给所有尚未检查的灯放上检查标记。其他动作、标记、玩家、顺序与四次期限不变。
第一步，甲检查两盏，左、右都变成已检查。第二步，乙点亮左灯。第三步，甲点亮右灯，两灯都亮，立即成功，不再进行第四步。
两版都表现“先检查，才能启用”。第一版把每盏灯的准备分别计时；第二版把一次检查视为覆盖整批的工作。两版没有不同数量的灯或不同目标，完成所需行动却从四次变成三次。
这说明从题材走到规则，还必须决定一个动作的对象和范围。“检查”这个动词本身，没有规定应该检查一盏还是一批。
关系怎样进入了桌面
玩家的角色是布置员，动作是检查与点亮，压力是四次行动。三者通过一个具体条件连接：亮灯标记只能放在已有检查标记的灯上。 读者现在既能执行它，也能核对它是否被遵守。
如果检查标记根本不影响点灯，也不影响其他结果，那么它在这个模型里就不会限制行动。多写几句“布置员认真工作”的故事，无法替这个标记补上作用。
但条件明确也不代表设计已经有足够的取舍。第一版没有故障、插队任务或信息变化，四次必要工作并不构成丰富的策略；第二版更快，也不自动更有趣。要加入另一项工作之前，先想清楚希望玩家为什么犹豫，别只因为题材里还有很多物件就全加进去。
自查：必须检查完，马上点亮吗？
回到第一版。如果甲先检查左灯，乙接着检查右灯，再由甲点亮右灯、乙点亮左灯，能否成功？
能，第四次行动后成功。 两次点亮发生时，对应的检查标记都已经存在，而且没有过期。规则只规定每盏灯内部的先后关系，没有要求检查和点亮紧挨着，也没有规定必须先完成左灯。
把这一步带回自己的题材
当你想表现一个关系，试着把它说成可核对的变化：谁操作哪个对象，什么条件满足后才能做，做完留下什么，再花掉多少机会。接着走两条合法过程，看看规则是否保留了你在意的关系，同时留下了怎样的自由。
给别人看这段原型时，可以观察他们是否知道为什么未检查的灯不能点亮。如果他们只是背出动作顺序，却说不清标记有什么作用，下一稿要先让这个条件更清楚。模型的目的在于表现一项准备关系，没有模拟真实灯具的检查项目、耗时或技术要求。
参考线索
Kathleen Mercury, Theme Research，Step #4、Alternative Step #4 与 Step #5；Choosing Your Mechanics。灯节模型、两版过程及分析为本站原创。
From Theme to Rule: Making “Prepare Before Use” Work

“Make a game about a lantern festival” gives us a setting, but it does not yet tell players what they can do. We can draw lanterns, stalls, and organizers. What must happen first, though, and who spends time on it? Relationships like these begin to turn a theme into rules that can run.
The original preparation model below retains just one relationship: a lantern must be checked before it can be lit. The checking conditions and four-action deadline are invented for this model.
Choose a relationship worth representing
Two players, organizers A and B, share the task of preparing the left and right lanterns before opening. They have a common goal and do not score individually.

We want preparation to matter. Checking therefore leaves a visible marker, and that marker determines whether lighting is allowed. Checking is now more than work mentioned in the story: it changes what can happen next.

The deadline gives that work a cost. An action spent checking cannot also be used for something else. We have not yet decided how much one check covers. Start with a version that handles lanterns individually.
Version one: check each lantern separately

Prepare two lantern cards, both unchecked and unlit. Place two check markers and two light markers beside them. All states are public, and there are no random events. Players may discuss their plans, and either player can work on either lantern.
Players act in the order A, B, A, B: at most four team actions. Each action is exactly one of these:
Check: place a check marker on one unchecked lantern.
Light: place a light marker on one checked but unlit lantern.
Wait: change nothing, using up the action.

Check markers do not expire and are not consumed by lighting. There is no movement, payment, or extra action. An unchecked lantern cannot be lit. As soon as both lanterns are lit, the team succeeds and stops. If the fourth action ends without that result, the team fails. There are no individual rankings or ties.
Here is one complete sequence:
Action · What the player does · State afterward
1, A · Check the left lantern · Left checked; both unlit
2, B · Light the left lantern · Left lit; right unchecked
3, A · Check the right lantern · Left lit; right checked
4, B · Light the right lantern · Both lit; success

Each lantern needs one check and one lighting action. Finishing both therefore requires at least four actions. This sequence uses the entire budget. That is not because the rules demand this exact script. Someone must perform all four necessary pieces of work.
Version two: check the whole batch

Change only the scope of checking. If any lantern remains unchecked, one check action now places a check marker on every unchecked lantern. Keep the other actions, markers, players, turn order, and four-action limit.
First, A checks both lanterns. Second, B lights the left one. Third, A lights the right one. Both are lit, so the team succeeds immediately; there is no fourth action.

Both versions represent preparation before use. The first accounts for each lantern's preparation separately. The second treats inspection as a single job covering the batch. The number of lanterns and the goal are unchanged, yet the required work falls from four actions to three.
A theme therefore leaves another decision for the designer: what is the target and scope of an action? The verb “check” does not specify whether it covers one lantern or a batch.
How the relationship reaches the table

The players are organizers. They check and light lanterns under a four-action limit. One concrete condition connects these things: a light marker can only be placed on a lantern that already has a check marker. A reader can now carry out the rule and verify that it has been followed.

If the check marker affects neither lighting nor any other result, it imposes no action constraint in this model. Additional sentences about diligent organizers cannot give the marker a function that the rules omit.

Clear conditions do not guarantee interesting decisions, however. Version one has no faults, competing jobs, or changing information. Its four necessary tasks do not provide rich strategy. Version two is faster, but that does not automatically make it more enjoyable. Before adding another job, decide why you want players to hesitate. A setting having many objects is not sufficient reason to include them all.
Check: must lighting immediately follow checking?
Return to version one. A checks the left lantern; B checks the right. A then lights the right lantern, and B lights the left. Does the team succeed?

Yes, after the fourth action. Each lighting action has the corresponding check marker available, and neither marker has expired. The rule specifies an order within each lantern's preparation. It does not require checking and lighting to be consecutive, or demand that the left lantern be completed first.
Bring this step to your own theme

To represent a relationship, describe a change someone can verify: who acts on which object, what must already be true, what remains afterward, and how many opportunities the action uses. Then follow two legal sequences. Examine which relationship the rules preserve and which freedoms remain.

When showing this prototype to someone, observe whether they understand why an unchecked lantern cannot be lit. If they merely repeat an action sequence without understanding the marker's role, make that condition clearer in the next version. This model represents a preparation dependency; it does not model real inspection procedures, durations, or technical requirements.
Reference leads
Kathleen Mercury, Theme Research, Step #4, Alternative Step #4, and Step #5; Choosing Your Mechanics. The lantern model, compared sequences, and analysis are original to this site.
主题的承诺：回到营地，就一定算完成了吗？
看到帐篷，人可能想到休息、集合或保管物品。这样的联想能帮助理解场景，却不能替游戏决定帐篷究竟有什么效果。读者带来的知识与规则实际允许的事情，可能只对上了一部分。
这里用一个原创的样本登记模型，区分三件事：故事让人期待什么、规则规定什么，以及玩家因此选择了哪一步。
先把真实起效的规则说清楚
一名玩家扮演考察员，正站在营地外，携带两枚样本标记。营地就在相邻的一格，登记栏目前为空。所有信息公开，没有其他角色、随机事件或样本来源，只剩两次行动。
每次可以选择一个合法动作：
回营：人在营地外时，移动到营地；携带的样本仍放在“手中”栏。
登记：人在营地时，把手中所有样本移到“已登记”栏，每枚得到 1 分。
等待：位置与样本不变，用掉一次行动。
每个动作都花一次机会，没有附加费用。第二次行动结束就停止；未登记样本收回盒中，不得分。没有对手或平手处理，这个片段比较的是最终登记所得的分数。样本只能登记一次，放在帐篷图案旁边不产生额外效果。
两种理解，走出两条过程
假设画面只醒目地写着“把样本带回家”，帐篷又占据了大部分空间。一个人可能把“到了营地”理解成“任务已经完成”。下面是据此构造的过程，并非实际试玩记录。
第一步，他回营。人到了帐篷，两枚样本仍在手中。第二步，他等待。片段结束，两枚未登记样本回盒，最终 0 分。等待是合法的；失分不是因为他犯了非法操作，而是因为他预期的效果并没有写在回营动作里。
再看另一种呈现：把营地分成“带回的样本”和“已登记”两栏，并在回营说明旁写出“到营地不计分；登记后每枚 1 分”。规则仍是上面那一套。
现在构造另一条过程：第一步回营，两枚样本进入营地但仍未登记；第二步登记，两枚移入已登记栏，最终 2 分。
两条过程的起点、预算和得分规则相同，第二步分别是等待与登记。这个比较展示误判规则可能带来的后果，不证明每个人看见第一种画面都会误判，也不证明第二种呈现已经通过读者测试。
名称可以帮忙，效果仍要写出来
“回营”帮助我们记住移动的方向；“登记”帮助我们区分携带和已完成记录的样本。主题在这里有用，因为词语、位置和动作能够互相提醒。
问题出在把提醒当成了更多规则。“营地”不自动意味着样本永远保留，“家”也不自动意味着得分。同样，在另一个游戏里，“医院”不自动允许免费恢复，“仓库”不自动允许无限存放。每个效果都需要自己的条件与后果。
不必因此把所有东西改名为 A、B、C。更好的做法，是保留有帮助的情境，同时把最容易混淆的状态放到桌面上，让读者看见“在这里”和“已经完成”是两回事。
要改的是表达，还是规则？
如果你希望保留“带回之后，还要花时间整理”的取舍，可以调整名称、栏位与例子，让登记步骤更容易被发现。这没有增加动作，也没有改变分数。
如果你真正希望“一到营地就保留成果”，也可以改规则，让回营自动完成登记。但这已经改变了行动成本：原来需要回营和登记两步，现在一步就能取得这两枚样本的分数。它应当作为另一个版本检查，不能只换一句说明却让一部分人按新效果玩。
还要区分看懂与认同。一个人完全理解登记规则，仍然可能不喜欢额外花一步。那是对这种安排的评价，不应全归为阅读困难。
自查：把帐篷改名，分数会变吗？
玩家已经回营，手中仍有两枚样本，只剩最后一次行动。你把帐篷标题改成“安全营地”，其他规则完全不变。玩家如果等待，得几分？如果登记呢？
等待仍为 0 分，登记为 2 分。 新标题没有移动任何样本，也没有更改结束时的处理。若标题让人以为等待也能保留成果，需要修正的是标题与效果的关系，不能暗中给它另加一条规则。
回到你的设计
给读者看一个动作之后的局面，请他先说下一步会允许什么、哪些成果已被保留，再一起走到结算。记录他的预期具体在哪个状态上与规则不同。这样才能区分词语误导、关键信息不显眼和规则本身不合期待。
这个模型没有模拟真实考察机构的样本管理流程。它只是用一个可算清的关系说明：主题能引导理解，而“我以为会这样”仍需要与实际规则核对。
参考线索
Kathleen Mercury, Theme Research，开头关于主题语境与先前知识的段落。
Paul Booth. Game Play: Paratextuality in Contemporary Board Games. Bloomsbury Academic, 2015. “Ludic Interaction in Doctor Who,” pp. 183–185. 本文的营地模型与两种理解为原创分析，不是书中案例或真人观察。
A Theme's Promise: Does Reaching Camp Mean You Are Done?

A tent may suggest rest, gathering, or keeping things safe. Those associations can make a setting understandable, but they cannot decide what the tent actually does in a game. A reader's prior knowledge may match only part of the rules.
This original sample-recording model separates three things: what the story invites someone to expect, what the rules specify, and which action a player chooses as a result.
Establish which rules actually take effect

One player is a researcher standing outside camp, carrying two sample markers. Camp is one adjacent space away. The recorded-samples area is empty. All information is public. There are no other characters, random events, or sources of samples. Two actions remain.
Each action is one legal choice:
Return: while outside camp, move into camp. Carried samples remain in the “In hand” area.
Record: while at camp, move all carried samples to “Recorded,” scoring 1 point per sample.
Wait: leave position and samples unchanged, using an action.

Each choice costs one action, with no additional payment. Stop after the second action. Unrecorded samples go back into the box and score nothing. There is no opponent or tie rule: this episode compares the final score from recorded samples. Each sample can be recorded only once. Placing it beside the tent illustration has no extra effect.
Two interpretations, two sequences

Suppose the prominent instruction says “Bring the samples home,” while a large tent fills most of the display. Someone might interpret reaching camp as completing the task. The following sequence is constructed from that possible interpretation; it is not a playtest record.

First, the player returns. The researcher is at the tent, but both samples remain in hand. Second, the player waits. The episode ends, both unrecorded samples return to the box, and the score is 0. Waiting was legal. The problem was an expected effect that the Return action does not provide.

Now consider a different display. Divide camp into “Samples brought back” and “Recorded,” and place this explanation beside Return: “Arriving at camp scores nothing. Record samples to score 1 point each.” Keep all the rules above.
Construct a second sequence. First, return: both samples are at camp but remain unrecorded. Second, record: move both into Recorded and finish with 2 points.

The starting position, action budget, and scoring rules match. The second actions differ: Wait and Record. This comparison demonstrates a possible consequence of misreading a rule. It does not show that everyone will misunderstand the first display, or that the second has passed a reader test.
Names help, but effects still need rules

“Return” helps us remember where the researcher moves. “Record” helps distinguish carried samples from completed records. The theme is useful here because words, locations, and actions can reinforce one another.

The problem is treating those reminders as additional rules. “Camp” does not automatically make samples permanent, and “home” does not automatically award points. Similarly, in another game, a hospital does not automatically grant free recovery, nor does a warehouse automatically permit unlimited storage. Each effect needs its own conditions and consequences.

There is no need to rename everything A, B, and C. Retain the helpful setting while making easily confused states visible. Let readers see the difference between being somewhere and having completed a task.
Does the presentation need changing, or the rule?
If you want players to spend time organizing samples after returning, improve the names, spaces, and examples so that recording is easier to notice. This adds no action and changes no score.

If you actually want arrival to secure the results, you can change Return so that it automatically records samples. That changes the action cost: what previously required returning and recording now takes one action to score both samples. Check it as a separate version. Do not merely change a sentence while some players continue using the old effect.

Understanding and agreement are different, too. Someone may understand recording perfectly and still dislike spending an extra action on it. That is an evaluation of the design, not necessarily a reading problem.
Check: does renaming the tent change the score?
The researcher has returned, still holds two samples, and has one action left. Rename the tent “Safe Camp,” leaving every rule unchanged. What does the player score by waiting? What about recording?

Waiting still scores 0; recording scores 2. The new heading moves no samples and does not alter their treatment at the end. If it suggests that waiting preserves them, revise the relationship between the heading and the effect. Do not silently invent another rule for it.
Bring it back to your design

Show a reader the position after an action. Ask what becomes possible next and which results are already secured, then follow the rules through resolution together. Record the specific state where the expectation differs from the rule. That helps distinguish misleading words, overlooked information, and a rule that does not match what the reader wants.

This model does not simulate a real research organization's sample-handling procedures. It uses one traceable relationship to show how a theme can guide understanding while still requiring expectations to be checked against the rules.
Reference leads
Kathleen Mercury, Theme Research, opening passages on thematic context and prior knowledge.

Paul Booth. Game Play: Paratextuality in Contemporary Board Games. Bloomsbury Academic, 2015. “Ludic Interaction in Doctor Who,” pp. 183–185. The camp model and compared interpretations are original analysis, not examples from the book or observations of real players.
比较两款游戏：出牌前，玩家究竟知道什么？
看到一张牌成功接上桌面，你可能想说：“玩家判断对了。”先把镜头倒回他决定出牌的时刻：当时知道什么？哪些事情还没有决定？成功有时来自充分的信息，有时只是结果恰好有利。
这次用《6 nimmt!》与《Hanabi》回答同一个问题：玩家承诺出牌前，能把后果判断到什么程度？两者都用牌，却有不同目标：前者尽量少收牛头罚分，后者共同接好五种颜色的烟花。我们比较一个决定中的信息，不把两局的分数或整体难度排在一起。
下面均为依照文末指定基本规则构造的新局面，未改变规则，也不加入过河游戏。每段只走到写明的观察终点，实际游戏仍会继续。
6 nimmt!：知道自己的牌，还缺什么？
两名玩家各有八张手牌，当前都没有收走的牌。本课固定甲选25，比较乙从同一手牌选23或35的两条过程；甲不知道乙的选择。双方各暗选一张，再一起揭示，按数字从小到大处理。数字牌没有重复，因此这里没有同数字的平手。
桌面四行如下，括号是这些牌上的牛头数量：
行 · 从左至右
一张牌必须接在“小于自己、又最接近自己”的行尾后。如果那里已有五张，就收走原来的五张，把自己的牌留下重开这一行。收走的牌进入个人牛头堆，不回手牌；牛头在本轮结束时合算罚分。小于全部行尾的牌须另选一行收走，本次两条过程不会触发它。
过程一：乙出23。23先接在20后，B行达到五张。接着处理甲的25，最接近的较小行尾是23，甲必须去B行。甲收走12、15、18、20、23，新增牛头是 1＋2＋1＋3＋1＝8。25留下，不能连它自己的两个牛头也算进去。
过程二：从原桌面重新开始，乙改出35。25先接在20后，成为第五张，甲不收牌。随后35必须接在25后，这次由乙收走12、15、18、20、25，新增牛头是 1＋2＋1＋3＋2＝9。35留下成为B行首。
两张都处理完，观察结束。两人手牌都从八张变七张，不补牌；A、C、D行不变。第一条过程B行只剩25，甲新增8个牛头；第二条只剩35，甲新增0、乙新增9。
甲两次都知道自己出了25，也看得见同一张桌面。缺的是乙尚未揭示的行动，以及那个行动会在何时更新桌面。“现在还有一个空位”没有替甲预留位置。这两条过程没有给乙选择23或35的概率，不能据此说甲有一半机会收牌。
Hanabi：看见成功，还不能确定什么？
仍用两名玩家，这次轮到米娅，随后轮到里奥。每种颜色都要按1、2、3、4、5接牌，不能跳号或重复。两人各五张牌，牌面朝向别人，自己看牌背。红色烟花只有红1，其余颜色尚未开始；可用提示标记为3，错误标记为0，牌堆剩39张，没有弃牌。
为了检查过程，给读者看里奥从左至右的牌：红2、绿1、黄4、白5、红4。里奥本人看不见。他记得先前完整的数字提示：只有第一张是2，此后手牌没有变化。第一张颜色仍未知；其他公开信息也没有排除蓝2等可能。
提示占用米娅整个行动，并花一个提示标记。她只能说一种颜色或一个数字，要同时指出所有符合的牌。收到提示后，里奥仍自己决定做什么。本例只按提示的字面信息推理，没有另加暗号、语气暗示或“她这样提示就是叫我出牌”的约定。
过程一：米娅提示红色。她必须指出第一和第五张，标记从3减为2，烟花不变。里奥把“第一张是2”和“第一张是红色”合起来，知道它正好接在红1后。他出第一张，红色烟花前进到2。
过程二：重置到原局面，米娅改提示数字4。她必须指出第三和第五张，同样花一个标记。第一张仍只知道是2，颜色没有补齐。如果里奥仍出第一张，实际翻出的也是红2，烟花照样前进到2。但这次成功不能证明他出牌前已经知道它能接上：若第一张是他尚未排除的蓝2，蓝色还没有1，就会接不上。
接不上的牌会弃掉并增加一次错误，第三次错误立即结束游戏。本次实际两条过程都成功，错误仍为0。里奥随后从牌堆抽一张，仍不看牌面；为固定比较，两条都设这张为黄1。牌堆39变38，他仍有五张牌。两条都在补牌后结束观察：红色到2、提示剩2、错误为0，却经历了不同的信息依据。
第二条不是推荐动作，也没有给猜中概率。它让你看到：相同的成功结果，不足以说明玩家当时拥有相同的判断依据。这里给提示不改烟花，随后由接收者行动；这不表示Hanabi所有回合的桌面都不变。
把比较写成能检查的结论
现在再把两款放在一起：
要检查什么 · 本次6 nimmt!片段 · 本次Hanabi片段
决定者已经知道什么 · 自己的25与当前四行 · 目标牌是2与公开烟花
还缺哪部分 · 对手本次选牌及其结算影响 · 自己目标牌的颜色
什么能补足判断 · 揭示并逐张更新桌面，但承诺已经作出 · 在出牌前取得完整颜色提示
单看结果会漏掉什么 · 甲没改选牌，对手仍能改变其代价 · 同样出成功，依据仍可能不同
比较时先写决定发生的时点，再列出玩家当时能用的信息，最后把结果走完。这样得到的是一段可以检查的因果关系。“一个有竞争、一个有合作”提供背景，还没有解释这次决定。8个牛头与一次烟花进展也不是同一种收益，不能用大小判定哪款更公平或更有趣。
这些局面支持规则分析，不证明作者当初为什么采用它们。若要比较人的理解，还要观察他在承诺前怎么解释可能结果；只看最后成功与否不够。
自查：换一个细节，结论还成立吗？
乙把23换成24，甲仍出25，会怎样？24先填第五位，甲仍收走五张。24有一个牛头，新增总数仍为8；关键是较小牌先填满这一行，不是数字必须恰好为23。
里奥只有“第一张是2”的信息，出牌成功就能证明提示已经充分吗？不能。第二条过程已经给出反例：红2恰好成功，但他的已知信息还允许接不上的蓝2。评价信息是否足够，要回到出牌前可以排除什么。
官方规则与本课范围
AMIGO：6 nimmt!英文基本规则，Version 2.10：第1页选牌、升序、最小差值与满行；第2页低牌、牛头数及轮末计分。本课不用专业变体。
Cocktail Games：Hanabi 2019年法文基本规则：第2—5页手牌方向、提示、出牌和序列；第6页结束；第8页允许各桌自行约定交流方式。本课采用上文写明的字面提示方式，不把它说成所有玩家唯一可用的约定。
Compare Two Games: What Does the Player Know Before Playing?

When a card fits successfully on the table, you might conclude that the player judged correctly. Rewind to the decision. What did that player know then? What was still undecided? Success can follow sufficient information, or simply a favorable outcome.

We will use 6 nimmt! and Hanabi to examine one question: How much can a player determine about the consequences before committing a card? Both use cards, but their goals differ. In the first, players try to collect fewer bullheads as penalties; in the second, they cooperate to complete five colored fireworks. We will compare information within a decision, without ranking whole-game scores or difficulty.

The following situations are original constructions under the specified base rules. They do not change those rules or add anything to the crossing game. Each observation stops at a stated point; the actual games would continue.
6 nimmt!: You know your card. What is missing?

Two players each have eight cards in hand and no collected cards. Hold A's choice at 25 and compare B selecting 23 or 35 from the same hand, without A knowing which. Both choose one card face down, reveal together, and resolve the cards from lowest to highest. Numbers are unique, so there is no equal-number tie here.
The four rows are shown below. Parentheses give each card's bullhead count.
Row · Left to right

A card must follow the row-end card that is lower than it and closest in value. If that row already has five cards, the player collects those five and leaves the played card to begin the row again. Collected cards enter the player's bull pile, never their hand; their bullheads become penalties when the round is scored. A card lower than every row end requires collecting a chosen row instead. Neither sequence here triggers that rule.

Sequence one: B plays 23. It follows 20 first, making row B five cards long. A's 25 is next. The closest lower row end is now 23, so A must use row B. A collects 12, 15, 18, 20, and 23, adding 1 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 8 bullheads. The 25 stays on the table; its own two bullheads are not collected.

Sequence two: reset the table and have B play 35 instead. The 25 follows 20 first as the fifth card, so A collects nothing. The 35 must then follow 25. B now collects 12, 15, 18, 20, and 25, adding 1 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 2 = 9 bullheads. The 35 becomes the new start of row B.

Stop observing after both cards resolve. Each hand falls from eight cards to seven, without drawing replacements; rows A, C, and D remain unchanged. In sequence one, row B contains only 25 and A has added eight bullheads. In sequence two it contains only 35; A has added zero and B has added nine.

A knows the chosen 25 and sees the same starting table in both sequences. The missing information is B's unrevealed action and when it will update the table. One currently empty slot does not reserve that slot for A. These sequences assign no probabilities to B choosing 23 or 35, so they do not establish a fifty-fifty chance of A collecting a row.
Hanabi: What does a successful play leave unproven?

Again there are two players: Mia acts, followed by Leo. Each color must follow the sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, without skipping or repeating a value. Each holds five cards facing outward, seeing their own card backs. The red firework contains only a red 1; the other colors have not started. Three clue tokens are available, no mistake tokens have been used, 39 cards remain in the deck, and the discard pile is empty.

For us to inspect the situation, here is Leo's hand from left to right: red 2, green 1, yellow 4, white 5, red 4. Leo cannot see those faces. He remembers an earlier complete number clue: only his first card is a 2. His hand has not changed since then. Its color remains unknown to him; other public information has not ruled out a blue 2, for example.

Giving a clue takes Mia's entire action and spends one clue token. She names one color or one number, indicating every matching card together. Leo still makes his own decision afterward. This example uses only the literal information in clues, without extra codes, emphasis, or an agreement that her choice of clue means he should play a particular card.

Sequence one: Mia clues red. She must indicate the first and fifth cards. Available tokens fall from three to two; the fireworks do not change. Leo combines “my first card is a 2” with “my first card is red.” It fits after the red 1. He plays it, advancing the red firework to 2.

Sequence two: reset the situation and have Mia clue 4 instead. She must indicate the third and fifth cards, again spending one token. Leo still knows only that the first card is a 2; its color remains unresolved. If he nevertheless plays that first card, it really is the red 2, so red again advances to 2. Success does not establish that he knew the card would fit. A blue 2, still consistent with his information, would not fit because the blue firework has no 1 yet.

A card that does not fit is discarded and adds a mistake; the third mistake ends the game immediately. Both actual sequences here succeed, leaving zero mistakes. Leo then draws without looking at the new face. To keep the comparison fixed, the replacement is a yellow 1 in both sequences. The deck falls from 39 to 38 cards and his hand returns to five. Stop observing after this draw: red is at 2, two clues remain, and there are no mistakes in either sequence, but the information supporting the plays differed.

The second sequence is not a recommended move, and we have assigned no probability of guessing correctly. It demonstrates that the same successful outcome does not establish the same information before the decision. Here the clue leaves the fireworks unchanged and its recipient acts next. This does not mean Hanabi's table remains unchanged across all turns.
Turn the comparison into a claim you can check
Now place the two situations alongside each other.
What to examine · This 6 nimmt! situation · This Hanabi situation
What does the decision-maker know? · The chosen 25 and the current four rows · The target card is a 2, plus the public fireworks
What is missing? · The opponent's choice and its effect during resolution · The target card's color
What can complete the picture? · Reveal and update the rows, after commitment · Receive a complete color clue before playing
What would the outcome alone conceal? · A's choice can stay fixed while the opponent changes its cost · Successful plays can have different informational support

First locate the decision in time. Then list the information available to that player, and finally resolve the outcome. This produces a chain you can check. Competition and cooperation give background, but do not by themselves explain this decision. Eight bullheads and one step of fireworks are different kinds of results; their size cannot establish which game is fairer or more enjoyable.

These situations support rule analysis, without proving why their designers chose the rules. To compare people's understanding, also observe how they explain possible consequences before committing. The final success or failure is insufficient.
Check your understanding—with answers

B replaces 23 with 24 while A still plays 25. What happens? The 24 fills the fifth position first, so A still collects five cards. The 24 has one bullhead, leaving the added total at eight. The relevant relationship is a lower card filling the row first; the number need not be exactly 23.

Leo knows only that his first card is a 2. Does successfully playing it prove that the clues were sufficient? No. The second sequence is a counterexample: the actual red 2 succeeds, while his information still allows an unplayable blue 2. Evaluate information by returning to what could be ruled out before the play.
Official rules and scope

AMIGO: 6 nimmt! English base rules, Version 2.10: page 1 covers selection, ascending order, lowest difference, and full rows; page 2 covers low cards, bullheads, and round-end scoring. This lesson does not use the Pro Variant.

Cocktail Games: Hanabi French base rules, 2019: pages 2–5 cover hand orientation, clues, play, and sequences; page 6 covers ending; page 8 permits groups to set their communication conventions. This lesson uses the literal-clue approach specified above, without calling it the only permitted convention for every group.
动物主题：谁在行动，谁只是被我们看见？
画面上有狐狸和水獭，不代表玩家就在扮演它们。玩家也可能是照护者、观察者，或者讲动物故事的人。角色一变，应该由玩家决定的事情也会变：是动物往哪里走，还是我们去哪里观察？
本站的动物主题入口包括这些不同视角，不把它们归成一种机制。先看一个原创观察模型，体会“看见动物”与“控制动物”的区别。
两只动物，两轮记录
两名玩家甲、乙合作记录一只狐狸和一只水獭。地图只有北区和南区，每轮每区各有一只动物。为便于推演，位置按下表固定且公开；它是编写的事件表，不代表真实动物的移动规律。
轮次 · 北区 · 南区
第 1 轮 · 狐狸 · 水獭
第 2 轮 · 水獭 · 狐狸
记录表有四格：狐狸第 1 轮、狐狸第 2 轮、水獭第 1 轮、水獭第 2 轮。起初全部为空。目标是在两轮结束时填满四格，也就是两只动物都在两个时段被记录到。
每轮先甲后乙，每人只有一次拍摄机会，不用就失去，不能留到下一轮。拍摄时选北区或南区，在对应动物、对应轮次的格子放上标记。同一格已经有标记，再拍也不会增加一格。两人可以商量，也可以选择同一区；没有占位冲突、秘密信息、费用或随机抽取。
本模型不计赶路时间，玩家每次直接选拍摄区域。玩家不能移动动物；第一轮两人都用完或放弃自己的机会后，才按表切换到第二轮位置。第二轮两人结束后统一检查：四格都满则共同成功，否则共同失败，没有个人分数或平手。
过程一：四张照片，都追着狐狸
第一轮，甲、乙都拍北区。两张照片都是狐狸，但只能填上“狐狸第 1 轮”这一格。
第二轮，狐狸在南区，两人又都拍南区。这次填上“狐狸第 2 轮”。片段结束，虽然拍了四张照片，记录表只有 2 格完成，水獭两格都空，全队失败。
他们没有违反拍摄规则。问题是重复照片没有补足记录目标：更多同一时段的照片，在本模型里不等于更多不同的记录。
过程二：每轮都照顾到两个区域
起点、位置表和全部规则不变。第一轮甲拍北、乙拍南，分别填上狐狸第 1 轮、水獭第 1 轮。
第二轮仍是甲拍北、乙拍南，但动物已经交换位置，因此分别填上水獭第 2 轮、狐狸第 2 轮。四次拍摄填满 4 格，全队成功。
过程 · 第 1 轮拍摄区域：甲／乙 · 第 2 轮拍摄区域：甲／乙 · 最终记录
两人都追狐狸 · 北／北 · 南／南 · 狐狸两格，合计 2 格
每轮分开观察 · 北／南 · 北／南 · 两只动物各两格，合计 4 格
第二条过程没有更大镜头或更多机会。它改变了机会的分配，让同样四次行动回应了四项不同需要。
动物在规则里是什么角色？
这个模型里，玩家是观察者；动物是会随时段改变位置的记录对象。玩家选择镜头指向，不能命令动物走到镜头前。角色、动作与压力由一条规则连接：有限拍摄机会要覆盖不同动物、不同轮次的格子。
如果改为玩家扮演动物，动物的去向可能就成为玩家动作；如果改为照护者，则需要定义哪些行动影响哪些需求。这些都不能由一张动物插画自动推出。首先选择视角，才能决定哪些变化由玩家控制、哪些变化是他必须回应的处境。
记录目标也体现了设计者的选择。本例重视两个对象在两个时段的覆盖，所以重复同一格无用。若改成“照片越多越好”，两条过程都拍四张，原来的差别就会消失。不能把前一种目标说成动物主题唯一正确的目标。
模型选择了什么，又省略了什么？
狐狸和水獭在这里靠标签区分，没有不同身体能力、食物需求或物种行为。它表现的是观察视角与记录覆盖，不是生态系统。换成两位虚构人物，也能保留这套计数关系；这说明动物题材提供了一个可理解的观察场景，没有独占这种机制。
位置完全公开，也意味着此刻几乎没有寻找未知动物的挑战。若想让发现、辨认或接近成为主要体验，就要另外定义线索、信息获得或距离，不能只把表藏起来便声称模拟了真实观察。真实识别误差、惊扰和环境变化都未在本模型中表示。
自查：照片都有了，还缺哪一格？
第一轮甲拍北、乙拍南；第二轮两人都拍南。最终完成几格，是否成功？
完成 3 格，失败。 第一轮得到狐狸和水獭各一格；第二轮南区只有狐狸，两张照片共同对应狐狸第 2 轮。缺少的是水獭第 2 轮。照片总数仍是四，不能用总数替代缺失的记录。
回到你的动物游戏
可以先观察读者在描述一次行动时，是否分得清“我改变了动物的行为”与“我改变了自己关注的位置”。再看他为什么认为某份记录有价值。若角色和目标还说不清，增加物种名称与插画也不会补上这条关系。只有准备表现具体动物差异时，才围绕那项差异查可靠资料，并明确游戏保留了哪些条件。
参考线索

Animal Themes: Who Acts, and Who Is Being Observed?

A picture of a fox and an otter does not mean the players are those animals. Players could be caretakers, observers, or storytellers. A different role changes which decisions belong to the player: where the animal goes, or where we look for it.

This site's animal theme entry includes those different perspectives without treating them as one mechanism. An original observation model will show the difference between seeing an animal and controlling it.
Two animals, two rounds of records

Players A and B cooperate to record one fox and one otter. The map contains only North and South, with one animal in each area each round. To make the sequence traceable, the positions below are fixed and public. This is an invented event schedule, not a claim about real animal movements.
Round · North · South
1 · Fox · Otter
2 · Otter · Fox

The record sheet has four boxes: Fox Round 1, Fox Round 2, Otter Round 1, and Otter Round 2. All start empty. The goal is to fill all four by the end of round two: both animals must be recorded in both periods.

In each round, A acts before B. Each has one opportunity to take a photograph. An unused opportunity is lost, not carried into the next round. To photograph, choose North or South and mark the box for that animal in that round. Photographing an already marked box adds no further box. Players may discuss their plans and choose the same area. There is no blocking, secret information, payment, or random draw.

The model does not charge travel time: players simply choose an area for each photograph. They cannot move animals. After both first-round opportunities, the animals switch to their second-round positions. After both second-round opportunities, check the sheet. Four filled boxes mean shared success; otherwise the team fails. There are no individual scores or ties.
Sequence one: four photographs following the fox
In round one, both players photograph North. Both pictures show the fox, but they fill only Fox Round 1.

In round two, the fox is at South. Both players photograph South, filling Fox Round 2. The episode ends with four photographs but only two filled boxes. Both otter boxes remain empty, so the team fails.
No photography rule was broken. Repeated images simply did not complete the required coverage. In this model, more photographs of the same animal in one period do not create more distinct records.
Sequence two: cover both areas each round
Keep the starting state, position schedule, and all rules unchanged. In round one, A photographs North and B photographs South, filling Fox Round 1 and Otter Round 1.
In round two, A again chooses North and B South. The animals have switched, so these photographs fill Otter Round 2 and Fox Round 2. Four photographs fill all four boxes, and the team succeeds.
Sequence · Round 1 areas: A / B · Round 2 areas: A / B · Final records
Both follow the fox · North / North · South / South · Both fox boxes: 2 total
Cover both areas each round · North / South · North / South · Two boxes per animal: 4 total
The second sequence uses no larger lens or additional opportunity. It distributes the same four actions across four different requirements.
What role do animals play in the rules?

Here, players are observers. Animals are subjects whose positions change with the period. Players choose where to point the camera; they cannot order animals to move in front of it. One rule connects role, action, and pressure: limited photographs must cover different animals in different rounds.

If players were the animals, choosing an animal's destination might become a player action. If players were caretakers, the design would need to specify which actions affect which needs. Neither relationship follows automatically from an illustration. Choosing a perspective helps establish what players control and which circumstances they must respond to.

The recording goal is also a design choice. This model values coverage of two subjects in two periods, making duplicates unhelpful. If the goal instead rewarded every photograph, both sequences would produce four and the distinction would disappear. The first goal is not the only correct goal for an animal game.
What does this model retain and omit?

Fox and otter are distinguished by labels, without different physical abilities, food requirements, or species behavior. The model represents observation and coverage, not an ecosystem. Two fictional people could replace the animals while preserving the counting relationship. Animal subject matter offers an understandable observation setting; it does not own this mechanism.

Public positions also leave little challenge in finding unknown animals. If discovery, identification, or approach should be central, define clues, information gathering, or distance separately. Merely hiding the position table would not establish a realistic observation model. Real identification errors, disturbance, and environmental changes are not represented here.
Check: which record is missing?
In round one, A photographs North and B South. In round two, both photograph South. How many boxes are filled? Does the team succeed?

Three boxes are filled, so the team fails. Round one records both animals. In round two, South contains only the fox, and both photographs correspond to Fox Round 2. Otter Round 2 is missing. There are still four photographs; their total cannot substitute for the absent record.
Bring it back to your animal game

First observe whether a reader describing an action distinguishes changing an animal's behavior from changing where they direct attention. Then examine why the reader thinks a record matters. If role and goal remain unclear, additional species names and pictures will not establish the relationship. When you choose to represent a particular animal difference, research that difference using reliable sources and identify which conditions the game retains.

交通与运输：路程更短，为什么准时分反而更少？
运输不只是把车从一格移到另一格。运的是什么、要送给谁、什么时候才算交付，会决定为什么要走这段路。玩家可以扮演司机，也可以安排班次或调度车辆；这些视角需要不同的动作权限。
下面是一份原创配送片段。它用固定道路、装卸动作和两个截止时点，比较较早完成与较高准时分。地点、耗时和奖励均为虚构条件。
一辆车，两份不同的承诺
一名玩家调度一辆货车，最多装两件货。开始时车在仓库 W，车上为空；仓库有红、蓝两件货，信息全部公开，没有随机事件或其他车辆。道路如下，每条连接都能双向通行：
北店 N — 中站 J — 仓库 W — 南店 S
红货必须交到北店，在第 4 次行动结束前交付可得 3 分；蓝货交到南店，在第 3 次行动结束前交付可得 2 分。恰好在截止行动交付也算准时。迟到仍可交货，但该件得 0 分。
最多进行八次行动，每次只做一项：在仓库装入一件或两件待送货物，不超过载量；沿一条连接移动一站；在正确的目的地交付一件车上的货；或等待。以上每项都花一次行动，没有其他费用。到达不等于交付，移动不会自动卸货。
货物不能在中途转交或寄放。一件货交付后从车上移到对应店铺，不能再次计分。两件都交付，或第八次行动结束，两者先到就停止。最终比较准时分；已送达件数用于说明完成情况，不另加分。这里只有一名玩家，同分方案在这个评分规则下价值相同。
过程一：先送较近的南店
第一步装上两件货，再按以下过程走：
行动 · 动作 · 车上与交付结果
1 · 在 W 装两件 · 红、蓝都在车上
2 · W 到 S · 到南店，尚未交货
3 · 交蓝货 · 蓝准时，得 2 分；车上剩红
4 · S 到 W · 携带红货回到仓库
5 · W 到 J · 红仍在车上
6 · J 到 N · 到北店，尚未交红货
7 · 交红货 · 已过第 4 次期限，得 0 分；两件送完，结束
总计七次行动，走了四段道路，两件都送达，准时分是 2。
过程二：先履行北店的承诺
保持完全相同的货物、道路、载量、期限和奖励，只换配送顺序。
第一步仍在 W 装两件；第二步 W 到 J；第三步 J 到 N；第四步交红货，正好准时，得 3 分。第五步 N 到 J，第六步 J 到 W，第七步 W 到 S，第八步交蓝货。蓝货超过第 3 次期限，得 0 分；两件送完，结束。
这一过程用了八次行动，走五段道路，比第一条多一段，准时分却是 3。如果目标只是更早送完，第一条更好；按当前准时奖励，第二条分数更高。你必须先知道游戏在重视什么，才能判断哪一趟更值得安排。
压力来自哪些关系？
角色是调度者，动作包括装车、移动和交付。有限行动与不同截止时点构成压力。最关键的连接是：货物要在正确地点，用一次交付动作完成，才能检查是否准时。 地图上的位置与计分表上的承诺因此连了起来。
没有装车容量，带什么可能不成问题；没有装卸耗时，完成时刻又会不同。在本例里，两件一起装不会额外增加行动，所以两条过程都固定使用合装，集中比较先去哪家。不能据此说所有运输游戏中满载都最好。
这也不是路线建设。道路一开始就存在，玩家没有修路动作；他是在既有连接上安排次序。若以后允许建桥或加站，就要说明建设如何改变行程，以及它本身花什么成本。
不是把所有现实问题塞进一辆小车
我们没有计算燃料、路况、装卸设备或车辆损耗，也没有把一步换算成真实分钟。3 分和 2 分只是这里对两项承诺的奖励安排，不是现实运输价格。
模型保留了货物、目的地和期限之间的关系。若主题换成接送乘客，还会出现这个模型没有表达的等待、上下车和人的需要，不能只把货物方块改叫乘客，就声称这些关系都已表现出来。
自查：提前到站就能得分吗？
车在第三次行动到达北店，第四次等待，第五次才交红货，红货得几分？另有没有办法让两件货都准时？
红货得 0 分。 截止条件看交付动作，而不是到站动作。
在给定起点和动作成本下，两件也不可能同时准时：先交蓝货最早要到第 3 次，之后经 S、W、J、N 并交红货，最早已是第 7 次；先交红货最早到第 4 次，蓝货的第 3 次期限已经过去。这是模型特意留下的冲突，不是靠“再算仔细一点”就能消失。
回到你的运输游戏
可以观察玩家是否区分了“车到了”“货交了”和“承诺完成了”。当他选择一条行程，问他比较的是路段数、完成时刻还是奖励。若两人说的“效率”指不同事情，先把目标和计分条件摆清楚，再决定要不要增加拥堵或更多车辆。

Transportation: Why Can the Shorter Trip Earn Fewer On-Time Points?

Transportation involves more than moving a vehicle between spaces. What is carried, who needs it, and when delivery counts determine why the journey matters. Players might drive, schedule services, or dispatch vehicles. Those perspectives need different action permissions.

This original delivery episode uses fixed roads, handling actions, and two deadlines to compare earlier completion with a higher punctuality score. Its locations, durations, and rewards are fictional.
One vehicle, two different commitments

One player dispatches a truck with capacity for two parcels. It starts empty at warehouse W, where red and blue parcels await collection. Everything is public; there are no random events or other vehicles. Every road below works in both directions:
North shop N — Junction J — Warehouse W — South shop S

Red goes to North and earns 3 points if delivered by the end of action 4. Blue goes to South and earns 2 points if delivered by the end of action 3. Delivery on the deadline action counts as punctual. Late delivery remains legal but earns 0 for that parcel.

There are at most eight actions. Each does exactly one thing: at W, load one or two waiting parcels without exceeding capacity; move along one connection; deliver one carried parcel at its correct destination; or wait. Each choice costs one action, with no other payment. Arrival is not delivery: movement never unloads automatically.

Parcels cannot be transferred or stored elsewhere en route. Delivery moves a parcel from the truck to its shop, and it cannot score again. Stop when both parcels are delivered or action eight ends, whichever happens first. Compare final punctuality points. The delivered count describes completion but earns no extra points. There is one player; plans with equal points have equal value under this scoring rule.
Sequence one: serve the nearer South shop first
Load both parcels, then follow this sequence:
Action · Move or task · Cargo and delivery result
1 · Load both at W · Red and blue aboard
2 · W to S · At South; nothing delivered yet
3 · Deliver blue · On time: 2 points; red remains aboard
4 · S to W · Return carrying red
5 · W to J · Red remains aboard
6 · J to N · At North; red not delivered yet
7 · Deliver red · After action 4: 0 points; both delivered, stop
This takes seven actions and traverses four road connections. Both parcels arrive, with a punctuality score of 2.
Sequence two: honor North's commitment first
Keep the parcels, roads, capacity, deadlines, and rewards identical. Change only delivery order.

Action 1 still loads both at W. Action 2 moves W to J; action 3 moves J to N. Action 4 delivers red exactly on time for 3 points. Action 5 moves N to J, action 6 J to W, and action 7 W to S. Action 8 delivers blue late for 0. Both are delivered, so stop.

This takes eight actions and five road connections—one more connection than the first sequence—but scores 3. If the goal were simply to finish sooner, the first sequence would be preferable. Under the current punctuality rewards, the second scores higher. You must know what the game values before deciding which journey is worth arranging.
Which relationships create the pressure?

The player is a dispatcher. Actions include loading, moving, and delivering. Limited actions and different deadlines create pressure. The critical connection is this: cargo must reach the correct place and use a delivery action before punctuality is checked. A map position now connects to a commitment on the scoring schedule.

Without a carrying limit, what to bring might cease to matter. Without handling time, completion times would change. Here, loading both parcels costs no extra action, so both sequences hold that decision constant and compare which shop to visit first. This does not establish that a full load is always best in every transportation game.

This is not route building, either. The roads already exist, and the player has no construction action. They schedule movement over fixed connections. Adding bridges or stops later would require rules for how construction changes journeys and what it costs.
A small truck need not contain every real-world issue

The model does not calculate fuel, traffic conditions, loading equipment, or vehicle wear. An action is not converted into real minutes. The rewards of 3 and 2 points are this model's treatment of two commitments, not real transportation prices.

What it preserves is a relationship among cargo, destinations, and deadlines. Changing the theme to passenger services would introduce waiting, boarding, and human needs that this model does not represent. Renaming parcels as passengers would not automatically represent those relationships.
Check: does arriving early secure the points?
The truck reaches North on action 3, waits on action 4, then delivers red on action 5. What does red score? Separately, can both parcels be delivered on time?
Red scores 0. The deadline checks delivery, not arrival.

Both cannot be punctual under these starting conditions and action costs. Delivering blue first takes at least three actions. Traveling S, W, J, N and delivering red then finishes no earlier than action 7. Delivering red first finishes no earlier than action 4, after blue's action-3 deadline has already passed. This conflict is deliberately present in the model; more careful arithmetic cannot remove it.
Bring it back to your transportation game

Observe whether players distinguish the vehicle arriving, the cargo being delivered, and a commitment being fulfilled. When a player chooses an itinerary, ask whether they are comparing road connections, completion time, or rewards. If two people mean different things by “efficiency,” clarify goals and scoring before adding congestion or more vehicles.

行动选择：一个动作为什么现在能选、等会儿却不能？
规则列着“移动、生产、升级”，还不足以说明玩家这一刻能做什么。动作可能仍印在面前，却因费用、先决条件、被别人取走，或自己刚刚用过而暂时不可选。设计行动系统，要同时说明动作的效果和进入这个动作的条件。
这是总览，不是一种固定机制
行动选择在这里是一个设计问题：行动怎样提供给玩家，又怎样受到限制？几种机制可以回答同一个问题，也可以一起使用。
提供行动的办法 · 选择前需要检查什么 · 选择后什么会变化
行动点预算 · 剩余点数能否支付费用，其他条件是否满足 · 剩余预算改变，某些动作可能付不起
有限的公共行动池 · 需要的行动机会是否还在 · 取走的机会不再供其他人选择
个人行动卡与收回 · 卡是否可用，执行条件是否满足 · 用过的卡暂时不可选，需按规则收回
“播出一段节目”是动作内容；“播出卡用过后需要收回”是提供行动的办法。不要把两者合成一个模糊的“播出机制”，也不必把所有有选择的游戏都塞进同一个分类。
袖珍电台的四次行动
这是原创的单人局部阶段。玩家起初有 1 份素材、0 分；储备区另有 4 份素材，消耗区为空，电台尚未调校。三张个人行动卡起初都正面朝上：
录音：从储备区拿 2 份素材；储备不足 2 份时不可选。
播出：把自己 1 份素材放入消耗区，立即得 3 分；没有素材时不可选。
调校：不耗素材，把“已调校”记为是；此后每次播出得 5 分，已经拿到的分数不变。每阶段只能调校一次。
所有信息公开，没有随机结果。每次行动选一张符合条件的正面卡，完整执行后把它翻面。翻面的卡不可再选。另有两个不靠卡片的选择：收回，把所有翻面的卡翻回正面，且必须至少有一张翻面卡；等待，什么也不改变。它们各占一次完整行动，收回后不能立即再用一张卡。
恰好完成四次行动后结束，只记录已得分数，剩余素材不计分。素材不会自动补充或返回，翻面的卡也不会自动恢复。这个片段没有更大的胜负规则。
先播出，还是先调校？
从初始状态分别走两条路线。表中数字为“手中素材／累计分数”。
第几次行动 · 路线甲 · 结果 · 路线乙 · 结果
路线甲结束时，录音与播出卡翻面，调校卡仍正面；储备区剩 2 份、消耗区 2 份。路线乙的三张卡都已收回，储备区剩 2 份、消耗区 1 份；电台仍处于已调校状态，不能再次调校。两条路线都把原有的 5 份素材完整分配到了各区。
调校确实提高了单次播出的分值，却没有提高这条路线的总分。起初只有 1 份素材时，想在四次行动内完成调校和两次播出，还需要一次录音、一次收回，总共五次，来不及。原规则下本阶段最高可得 6 分；选择调校的路线最高为 5 分。
只改“用后翻面”，同样的素材能做什么？
重置初始状态，只让行动卡用后继续保持正面。费用、效果、四次行动上限、调校仅一次都不变。现在可以依次录音、调校、播出、播出：手中素材为 3、3、2、1，累计分数为 0、0、5、10。最后所有卡正面，储备区剩 2 份、消耗区 2 份。
在原规则下，同样先做录音、调校、播出，第三次行动后也有 2 份素材，但播出卡已经翻面。第四次可以收回，不能再次播出，最后只有 5 分。差别不是玩家突然拥有更多素材，而是素材够用时，行动资格是否仍然存在。
这个单人片段没有公共争抢，不能用它证明限制行动会增强玩家间互动。若改用公共行动池，还要写清谁先选、机会有几份，以及别人取走后自己还剩什么。
取舍依赖什么条件？
回到用后翻面规则，只把起始素材由 1 份改为 2 份。此时调校、播出、收回、播出合法，最后得 10 分，手中素材为 0，储备区仍有 4 份，消耗区有 2 份，播出卡翻面。因为省去录音，四次行动已经够用。
所以“先升级”不是永远正确或永远错误。本例真正要比较的是：有限行动次数内，准备、补给、恢复资格和产生收益能否排得下。若只看单次播出的 3 分与 5 分，就会漏掉其他动作占去的机会。
行动系统可以让可用机会清楚可见，也可能要求玩家反复检查卡面、资源与条件。增加动作名称不保证多出值得考虑的选择；如果一个动作在当前目标下始终更差，应直接承认，再决定要不要改变条件。
自查：够付款，就一定能行动吗？
原规则、初始 1 份素材，前三次依次录音、调校、播出。第四次能否再花 1 份素材播出？能否先收回，再立刻播出？
答案：都不能。此时有 2 份素材，但播出卡翻面；收回本身占最后一次行动。若选择收回，结束时仍为 5 分、2 份素材，三张卡正面，电台已调校。卡恢复可用不会自动执行其效果。
带回自己的设计
挑一个玩家常说“我想做，但不能做”的动作，分别检查：动作是否提供、能否付款、先决条件是否满足、是否还有执行机会。这样能分辨需要修改的是动作本身、提供办法，还是把条件说明得更清楚。观察时再记录玩家在哪一步停下来；本页的算例没有替真实玩家报告困难。
来源与范围

概念研究参考 Geoffrey Engelstein 与 Isaac Shalev，Building Blocks of Tabletop Game Design: An Encyclopedia of Mechanisms，第二版，CRC Press，2022，第 3 章 “Actions”，ACT-01 “Action Points”、ACT-02 “Action Drafting”、ACT-03 “Action Retrieval”。书中区分行动内容与提供方式，并讨论预算、共享机会和个人行动恢复。本页电台规则、数字、路线与条件比较均为本站原创分析。
“行动选择”在本页是跨机制的总览，未强配为一个 BGG 分类。具体预算机制可继续读行动点条目；公开位置的进入限制可与工人放置条目比较。
Action selection: why is an action available now but unavailable later?

A list of “move, produce, upgrade” does not yet tell us what a player can do at this moment. An action may still be printed in front of them but be unavailable because of its cost, a prerequisite, another player's choice, or their own previous use. Designing an action system means specifying both an action's effect and access to that action.
An overview, not one fixed mechanism
Here, action selection names a design question: how are actions offered and restricted? Different mechanisms can answer this question, and they can work together.
How actions are offered · What must be checked before choosing? · What changes afterwards?
An action-point budget · Can the remaining points pay the cost, and are other conditions met? · The budget decreases; some actions may become unaffordable.
A limited shared action pool · Is the required opportunity still available? · A taken opportunity is unavailable to other players.
Personal action cards with retrieval · Is the card available, and are its conditions met? · Used cards become unavailable until retrieved under the rules.

“Broadcast a program segment” describes an action's content. “Retrieve the broadcast card before using it again” describes how the action is offered. Avoid collapsing these into a vague “broadcast mechanism,” or treating every game with choices as one classification.
Four actions at a pocket radio station

This is an original single-player local phase. Start with 1 material token and 0 points. A reserve holds 4 more material tokens; the consumed area is empty and the station is not tuned. Three personal action cards begin face up:
Record: take 2 material tokens from the reserve. This is unavailable if fewer than 2 remain there.
Broadcast: move 1 of your material tokens to the consumed area and immediately score 3 points. You need a token to do this.
Tune: spend no material and mark the station as tuned. Every subsequent broadcast scores 5 points; previously earned points do not change. You may tune only once this phase.

All information is public, with no random outcomes. For each action, choose a face-up card whose conditions you meet, resolve it completely, and turn it face down. Face-down cards cannot be chosen. Two choices require no card: retrieve, turning all face-down cards face up, provided at least one is face down; and wait, changing nothing. Each takes one whole action. Retrieving does not let you immediately play another card.

The phase ends after exactly four actions. Record earned points; leftover material scores nothing. Material never refills or returns automatically, and used cards do not automatically recover. No larger game's victory condition is assumed.
Broadcast first, or tune first?
Run each route from the initial state. Numbers below mean “material held / cumulative points.”
Action number · Route A · Result · Route B · Result
1 · Broadcast · 0 / 3 · Tune · 1 / 0
2 · Retrieve · 0 / 3 · Record · 3 / 0
3 · Record · 2 / 3 · Broadcast · 2 / 5
4 · Broadcast · 1 / 6 · Retrieve · 2 / 5

Route A ends with Record and Broadcast face down and Tune face up. The reserve holds 2 tokens and the consumed area holds 2. Route B ends with all cards retrieved, 2 tokens in reserve, and 1 consumed. The station remains tuned: retrieving Tune does not permit another tune. Both routes account for all 5 original material tokens.

Tuning improves each broadcast's value without improving this route's total. Starting with only 1 material, tuning and broadcasting twice also require recording and retrieval: five actions, exceeding the four available. Under the original rules, the phase's maximum is 6 points. Routes that include tuning can score at most 5.
Change only whether a used card turns face down

Reset the starting state. Change one rule: cards now stay face up after use. Costs, effects, the four-action limit, and tuning only once remain unchanged. Record, tune, broadcast, broadcast is now legal. Material held progresses through 3, 3, 2, 1, while points progress through 0, 0, 5, 10. All cards finish face up; the reserve holds 2 tokens and the consumed area holds 2.

Under the original rules, the same first three actions—record, tune, broadcast—also leave 2 material tokens. However, Broadcast is face down. You can retrieve on action four, but cannot broadcast again, finishing on only 5 points. The difference is not additional material. It is whether an action remains available when its cost is affordable.

This single-player phase contains no competition for shared opportunities. It cannot establish that restricting actions increases interaction between players. A shared action pool would additionally need rules for selection order, available copies, and what remains after someone else chooses.
Which conditions change the tradeoff?

Restore the face-down rule and change only the initial material from 1 token to 2. Tune, broadcast, retrieve, broadcast is now legal. It ends on 10 points, with no material held, 4 tokens still in reserve, 2 consumed, and Broadcast face down. Omitting Record makes the plan fit into four actions.

“Upgrade first” is therefore neither always right nor always wrong. The relevant comparison is whether preparation, resupply, restored access, and scoring fit within the available actions. Comparing only the 3-point and 5-point broadcasts misses the opportunities consumed by other actions.

An action system can make opportunities visible, but it can also require repeated checks of cards, resources, and conditions. More action names do not guarantee more worthwhile decisions. If an action is consistently worse under the current objective, acknowledge that before deciding whether to change the conditions.
Check: does being able to pay guarantee access?

Use the original rules and start with 1 material token. Your first three actions are record, tune, broadcast. Can your fourth action spend another token to broadcast? Can you retrieve and immediately broadcast?

Neither is legal. You hold 2 material tokens, but Broadcast is face down. Retrieval itself uses the last action. If you retrieve, you finish on 5 points with 2 material tokens, all cards face up, and the station still tuned. Restoring an action's availability does not automatically perform it.
Bring the question to your design

Choose an action for which a player says, “I want to, but I cannot.” Check separately whether it is offered, affordable, permitted by its prerequisites, and still possible within the remaining opportunities. This distinguishes changing the action from changing access or explaining conditions more clearly. During observation, record where players actually pause. These calculations do not report difficulties experienced by real players.
Sources and scope

Conceptual research draws on Geoffrey Engelstein and Isaac Shalev, Building Blocks of Tabletop Game Design: An Encyclopedia of Mechanisms, second edition, CRC Press, 2022, chapter 3, “Actions”: ACT-01, “Action Points”; ACT-02, “Action Drafting”; and ACT-03, “Action Retrieval.” These sections distinguish action content from how actions are offered and discuss budgets, shared opportunities, and personal action recovery. The radio rules, values, routes, and conditional comparisons are original analysis.
This overview spans mechanisms and is not assigned a single BGG category. Continue to the action-points entry for budgets, or compare the worker-placement entry for access to public spaces.
行动点：预算够不够，还要看先后顺序
一回合能做四件事，不表示每个计划都装得下。动作可能成本不同，某一步还会改变位置、资源或后续资格。行动点把这些动作放进一个共同预算，也让“先做什么”成为需要算清的问题。
用点数购买行动机会
行动点（Action Points）让玩家获得一笔行动预算，再支付点数执行动作。有的动作都花 1 点，有的成本不同；可以用标记记录，也可以在规则中直接规定次数。点数本身不一定是游戏里的钱或最终分数。
完整规则还需说明：预算什么时候获得；能否重复动作；费用是否必须一次付清；何时轮到别人；未用点保留还是作废。下面采用“每回合新得 4 点，未用点作废”的一种实现，不把它当成全部行动点游戏的共同规定。
两回合的观测台
这是原创单人局部阶段，所有信息公开，没有随机结果。三个位置排成一条线：工作台—窗边—屋顶，只能在相邻位置之间移动。玩家起初在窗边，持有 1 张滤片，0 分；工作台储备有 2 张滤片，消耗区为空。窗边近景和屋顶远景都尚未记录。
阶段只有两个回合，每回合开始获得 4 行动点。回合内可按任意合法顺序执行下列动作，先付足点数，再处理效果：
动作 · 费用与条件 · 效果
移动 · 1 点 · 移到一个相邻位置，可重复
取滤片 · 1 点；必须在工作台且储备非空 · 从储备拿 1 张，可重复
记录近景 · 2 点；在窗边、有滤片且近景未记录 · 将 1 张滤片放入消耗区，标记近景已记录，得 4 分
记录远景 · 2 点；在屋顶、有滤片且远景未记录 · 将 1 张滤片放入消耗区，标记远景已记录，得 7 分
每个目标本阶段最多记录一次。可以主动结束回合；点数用完也结束。未用点立即作废，不能先付一部分，下回合再补足。位置、滤片、记录状态和已得分数保留。第二回合结束后阶段结束，剩余滤片和点数不计分。滤片消耗和分值都是本例设定。
先拿 4 分，反而留下两次记录的机会
第一回合先在窗边记录：花 2 点与 1 张滤片，得 4 分；再花 1 点去工作台、1 点取滤片。正好用完 4 点，结束时在工作台，有 1 张滤片，储备剩 1 张。
第二回合有新的 4 点。花 1 点到窗边、1 点到屋顶，再花 2 点与 1 张滤片记录远景。阶段结束时在屋顶，得 11 分，手中没有滤片，储备区 1 张、消耗区 2 张，两处都已记录。
若第一回合先去屋顶拿眼前的 7 分呢？移动花 1 点，记录花 2 点，剩下 1 点返回窗边。第二回合需先花 1 点去工作台、1 点取滤片、1 点回窗边，只剩 1 点，付不起记录近景的 2 点。此时结束，最后为 7 分，在窗边持有 1 张滤片，储备与消耗区各 1 张，近景仍未记录。
先近景的完整路线需要三步移动、一次取滤片、两次记录，共 3＋1＋4＝8 点。先远景再回来补近景至少需要四步移动，总计 9 点，超过两回合的 8 点。眼前较高分并非坏选项；如果只剩一个回合，先取远景的 7 分就比近景的 4 分高。改变判断的是剩余时间和路线。
只改未用点能否带走
重置初始状态，尝试另一条准备路线：第一回合去工作台、取滤片、回窗边，共花 3 点，持有 2 张滤片，尚未得分。按原规则，剩下 1 点作废，第二回合只有 4 点。
若第二回合按“记录近景、上屋顶、记录远景”的计划执行，费用是 2＋1＋2＝5。原规则下最后一步不合法：做完前两步只剩 1 点，只能以 4 分结束这条计划。也可以改选只记录远景，得到 7 分。
现在只让第一回合未用点保留，并与下回合新得的 4 点相加。准备路线剩的 1 点使第二回合有 5 点，原先装不下的三个动作可以完整执行。结束时得 11 分，在屋顶没有滤片，储备区 1 张、消耗区 2 张，两处都已记录，点数为 0。
变化是这条准备路线变得可行，不是整个片段的最高分从 4 变成 11：原规则的“先近景”路线本来就能得 11 分，两版最多也只有两个目标的 11 分。保留预算改变了可行计划，未必提高最高收益。
什么时候有用，代价又在哪里？
行动点适合让不同动作竞争同一笔预算，例如移动和使用地点的效果不能各算各的。不同费用能区分动作投入，但也要求玩家把路径、先决条件与剩余点数一起考虑。本例只会加减仍不够：先去哪里改变了需要走几步。
点数增加可能让组合终于完成，也可能只是让玩家在同一回合计算更多排列。若新增的动作始终没有收益，或者有一条路线在所有相关条件下都更好，多几个点不会自动产生丰富策略。应观察玩家实际比较了哪些计划、在哪一步发现费用不够，以及其他人等待了多久；单人算例不能回答最后一项。
也要分清行动点和普通资源。这里滤片跨回合保留，行动点默认不保留，两者共同决定记录是否可行。把点数改名为“能量”并不会自动决定能否储存；规则仍须写明。一个包含多个自动步骤的固定行动，也不能仅因步骤多就被当作玩家在分配预算。
自查：最后四点放在哪里？
仍按原规则。最后一回合开始时，你在工作台，持有 2 张滤片、4 行动点、0 分；储备剩 1 张，两处都未记录。比较“去窗边、记录近景、去屋顶”和“去窗边、去屋顶、记录远景”。能否两处都记？
答案：第一条花 1＋2＋1＝4 点，得 4 分；第二条花 1＋1＋2＝4 点，得 7 分。两条都在屋顶结束，手中剩 1 张滤片，储备与消耗区各 1 张，但记录完成的位置不同。两处都记至少要两次移动加两次记录，共 6 点，当前付不起。若只比较本阶段分数，这个局面应选第二条；不要为了宣称“都有取舍”而把 4 分与 7 分说成同样好。
来源与分类对照

概念研究参考 Geoffrey Engelstein 与 Isaac Shalev，Building Blocks of Tabletop Game Design: An Encyclopedia of Mechanisms，第二版，CRC Press，2022，第 3 章 ACT-01 “Action Points”。该条目讨论预算、不同成本、重复限制和未用点的处理，并提醒较大预算可能扩大决策量。本页观测台规则与全部路线核算为本站原创。
BGG：Action Points 用于分类身份对照；该名称不决定具体的行动费用、重复限制或点数保留规则。
Action points: a sufficient budget still needs the right order

Being able to do four things does not mean every plan fits. Actions may have different costs, and each step can change your position, resources, or access to the next one. Action points put these actions into a shared budget, making their order something to calculate.
Spend points on opportunities to act

Action points give a player a budget to spend on actions. Actions might all cost 1 point or have different costs. Points can be tracked with markers or expressed as a number of permitted actions. They need not represent money or final score.

Complete rules also specify when the budget arrives, whether actions may repeat, whether costs must be paid in full, when another player acts, and whether unused points carry over or expire. Our example grants 4 new points per turn and discards leftovers. This is one implementation, not a universal requirement.
Two turns at an observatory

This original single-player local phase has public information and no random outcomes. Three locations form a line: workbench—window—roof. Movement is only between adjacent locations. Start at the window with 1 filter and 0 points. The workbench reserve holds 2 filters; the consumed area is empty. Neither the near target at the window nor the far target on the roof has been recorded.
There are exactly two turns. Gain 4 action points at the start of each. Within a turn, perform actions in any legal order, paying their full point cost before resolving their effects:
Action · Cost and conditions · Effect
Move · 1 point · Move to an adjacent location; repeatable.
Collect a filter · 1 point; at the workbench with a nonempty reserve · Take 1 filter from the reserve; repeatable.
Record the near target · 2 points; at the window, with a filter, and near target not yet recorded · Move 1 filter to the consumed area, mark the near target recorded, and score 4.
Record the far target · 2 points; on the roof, with a filter, and far target not yet recorded · Move 1 filter to the consumed area, mark the far target recorded, and score 7.

Each target may be recorded only once this phase. You may end a turn voluntarily; spending all its points also ends it. Unused points immediately expire. You cannot partially pay now and complete payment next turn. Position, filters, recorded targets, and earned score persist. The phase ends after turn two; leftover filters and action points score nothing. Filter consumption and rewards are rules of this example.
Taking 4 points first leaves room to record twice

On turn one, record at the window: spend 2 action points and 1 filter to score 4. Spend 1 point moving to the workbench and 1 collecting a filter. All 4 points are spent. You finish at the workbench holding 1 filter, with 1 left in reserve.

Turn two supplies 4 new points. Spend 1 moving to the window, 1 moving to the roof, and 2 plus a filter recording the far target. The phase ends on the roof with a score of 11, no filters held, 1 in reserve, and 2 consumed. Both targets are recorded.

What if you take the immediate 7-point target first? On turn one, spend 1 to reach the roof, 2 to record, and the last 1 returning to the window. On turn two, moving to the workbench, collecting a filter, and returning to the window each cost 1. Only 1 point remains, insufficient for the 2-point near recording. End there: a score of 7, at the window holding 1 filter, with 1 each in reserve and consumed. The near target remains unrecorded.

The near-first route requires three moves, one collection, and two recordings: 3 + 1 + 4 = 8 points. Recording far first and returning to complete near needs at least four moves, totaling 9 points against an eight-point budget. The higher immediate reward is not inherently bad. With only one turn remaining, the far target's 7 beats the near target's 4. Remaining time and route change the judgment.
Change only whether unused points carry over

Reset the initial state and try another preparation route. On turn one, move to the workbench, collect a filter, and return to the window. This costs 3 points, leaving you with 2 filters and no score. Under the original rules, the unused point expires and turn two supplies only 4 points.

The intended second-turn plan—record near, move to the roof, record far—costs 2 + 1 + 2 = 5. Its last step is illegal under the original rules. After the first two steps, only 1 point remains, so this plan ends with a score of 4. You could instead choose to record only far, scoring 7.

Now change just one rule: unused turn-one points carry over and add to the next turn's 4 new points. The preparation route leaves 5 points for turn two, allowing all three planned actions. Finish on the roof with a score of 11, no filters held, 1 in reserve, 2 consumed, both targets recorded, and no action points left.

The preparation route has become feasible. The phase's overall maximum has not risen from 4 to 11: the original near-first route already scores 11, and the two targets cap both versions at 11. Saving a budget can change feasible plans without increasing the highest reward.
What does this mechanism offer and cost?

Action points let different actions compete for one budget. Moving and using a location's effect cannot be considered separately here. Different costs distinguish investment, but ask players to consider routes, prerequisites, and remaining points together. Addition and subtraction alone are insufficient: where you go first changes how many moves you need.

A larger budget might finally permit a combination, or merely add more sequences to consider during one turn. If extra actions offer no benefit, or one route is better under every relevant condition, additional points do not automatically create richer strategy. Observe which plans players compare, where they discover an unaffordable step, and how long others wait. A single-player calculation cannot answer that last question.

Distinguish action points from other resources. Filters persist between turns here; action points normally do not. Both affect whether recording is possible. Calling points “energy” does not determine whether they can be saved: the rule must specify it. Nor does one fixed action with several automatic steps become budget allocation merely because it contains many steps.
Check: where should the final four points go?

Use the original rules. At the start of the final turn, you are at the workbench with 2 filters, 4 action points, and a score of 0. The reserve holds 1 filter and neither target is recorded. Compare “move to window, record near, move to roof” with “move to window, move to roof, record far.” Can you record both?

Answer: the first route costs 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 and scores 4. The second costs 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 and scores 7. Both finish on the roof holding 1 filter, with 1 in reserve and 1 consumed, but different targets recorded. Completing both requires at least two moves and two recordings, costing 6 points, which you cannot afford. For this phase's score alone, choose the second route. Do not present 4 and 7 as equally good merely to claim that every decision is a tradeoff.
Source and classification

Conceptual research draws on Geoffrey Engelstein and Isaac Shalev, Building Blocks of Tabletop Game Design: An Encyclopedia of Mechanisms, second edition, CRC Press, 2022, chapter 3, ACT-01, “Action Points.” It discusses budgets, different costs, repetition limits, and unused points, and notes that larger budgets can expand the decision space. The observatory rules and all route calculations are original.
BGG: Action Points supplies a classification identity. The name does not determine particular action costs, repetition limits, or point-carryover rules.
手牌管理：这张牌现在用，下一轮还剩什么？
两张牌都能完成眼前的工作，是否随便出一张就好？先看一个差别：专用工具现在够用，万能工具以后还能应付另一种工作。出牌的结果不只是一笔分数，也包括下一轮还留下哪些选择。
三轮工作，只有三张工具卡
下面是自行构造的单人局部游戏，用来观察用牌、留牌与补牌。三轮工作提前公开：第 1 轮需要蓝工具，完成得 2 分；第 2 轮需要蓝工具，得 4 分；第 3 轮需要红工具，得 3 分。每轮的工作只在当轮有效，不能提前完成或留到以后。
起手有两张卡：蓝工具 B1，只能完成蓝工作；万能工具 W，可以完成红或蓝工作。桌上另有一张公开的蓝工具 B2，作为补充牌。除此以外没有牌，也没有隐藏信息。
每轮选择一次：从手中打出一张符合要求的牌，完成工作并得分；或者跳过，不得分。打出的牌放进弃牌区，本局不再回来。W 一次只能完成当前这一份工作。没有额外钱币费用。除了出牌，不能主动弃牌；也不能交换牌或从补充区直接用牌。
手牌上限为两张。仅在第 1 轮结束时检查一次：若手牌少于两张，把 B2 拿进手中；否则 B2 留在原处，之后没有补牌机会。第 3 轮结束即结算总分，余牌没有分数。目标是尽量多得分，同分的计划视为同样结果。
同得 2 分，留下的却不同
第一种过程先使用专用牌：
时点 · 选择与得分 · 之后的手牌
第 1 轮 · 用 B1 完成蓝工作，得 2 分；轮末补入 B2 · W、B2
第 2 轮 · 用 B2 完成蓝工作，得 4 分 · W
第 3 轮 · 用 W 完成红工作，得 3 分 · 空
总分是 9，三张牌全在弃牌区。再看另一种合法过程：第一轮用 W 得 2 分，补牌后留下 B1、B2；第二轮用 B1 得 4 分；第三轮 B2 无法完成红工作，只能跳过。总分是 6，弃牌区有 W、B1，手中还剩 B2。
第一轮两种出法的眼前收益完全相同。分数差别到第三轮才显现：用掉 W，也用掉了全局唯一能完成红工作的工具。留下一张牌不等于留下同等有用的选择；最后握着 B2，仍然没有合法的红工作出法。
这就是这里所说的手牌管理：安排手中可用选项的使用、保留和补充，连接现在的行动与以后的行动。它关注牌什么时候可用、用了以后去哪里，以及留下来的牌能做什么。
只把补牌推迟一轮
现在重开一局，只改一条规则：唯一的补牌检查从第 1 轮末移到第 2 轮末。牌、手牌上限、工作和分数都不变。
若第一轮仍用 B1 得 2 分，第二轮开始只有 W。想完成眼前价值 4 分的蓝工作，就必须用 W；随后拿到 B2，第三轮仍做不了红工作。结果是 6 分。如果第二轮跳过，留 W 做第三轮红工作，则是 2＋0＋3＝5 分。
另一个过程更好：第一轮跳过；第二轮用 B1 得 4 分，再补入 B2；第三轮用 W 得 3 分。结果是 7 分，B2 留在手中。这里跳过较小的眼前收益，保住了后面两份工作的配合。
延后补牌的版本最多得 7 分：要拿到最后的红工作分，必须留住 W；在 B2 到手前，两轮蓝工作只能用 B1 完成其中一轮，因此选择价值 4 分的第二轮。若 W 也拿去做蓝工作，两轮蓝工作合计只有 6 分。
两版始终只有三张牌。改变结果的是可用时点。B2 明明在桌上，也不能在它进入手牌之前帮忙。
它与其他卡牌概念哪里不同
这个局面没有洗牌，也没有随机抽取；手牌管理仍然存在。它也没有在游戏过程中改变会循环使用的牌库组成，因此不是在演示牌库构筑。W 有两种用途，只是让保留的代价更明显；即使每张牌只有一种用途，只要用途和使用时点不同，也会有留牌问题。
“多拿牌”与“把牌用好”也不是同一件事。两张蓝牌面对红工作都不合用；手牌上限只告诉你最多能留几张，没有告诉你该留哪张。设计时还要区分一次补几张、何时检查上限，以及超过上限时怎么处理。
这个小局面把未来全部摊开，所以能算出最高分。若未来工作隐藏，玩家就需要根据已知信息取舍，不能把事后看到正确答案等同于当时作了坏决定。若所有手牌总能无代价换成彼此，或每次用完立刻取回，保留的压力也可能减弱。
自查：一张都不出，就能多存一张吗？
回到原版。第一轮跳过，之后第二轮用 B1，第三轮用 W。结束时 B2 在哪里，总分是多少？
B2 仍在补充区。第一轮末手里有 B1、W，已满两张，唯一的补牌检查不会让 B2 入手。后两轮分别得 4 分和 3 分，总分为 7。结束时两张起手牌在弃牌区。没有出牌，也可能错过补充机会。
回到自己的设计，可以观察一次具体决定：玩家放弃了一张什么牌的未来用途？下一张牌到手之前，哪一次工作会先失效？如果玩家说“我有牌却什么也做不了”，先核对牌的用途、进入手牌的时点和行动条件，才能判断需要改牌的数量，还是改牌的流动规则。
参考与分类检索

Hand Management: What Will Be Left After You Play This Card?

If two cards can complete the current job, does it matter which one you play? A specialist tool may be enough today, while a flexible tool can handle a different job later. Playing a card changes both your score and the choices you will have next round.
Three rounds and three tool cards

This original solo example examines playing, keeping, and replenishing cards. All three jobs are visible from the start. Round 1 needs a blue tool and awards 2 points; round 2 needs a blue tool and awards 4; round 3 needs a red tool and awards 3. Each job is available only in its own round. You cannot complete it early or save it for later.

Your starting hand contains blue tool B1, which handles only blue jobs, and flexible tool W, which handles either red or blue. One more blue tool, B2, sits face up in a reserve. There are no other cards and no hidden information.

Each round, either play one suitable card from your hand to complete the job and score, or pass for no points. Played cards go to a discard area and never return during this game. W completes only the current job when played. There is no extra money cost. Cards cannot be discarded except by playing them; exchanging cards or playing directly from the reserve is not allowed.

The hand limit is two. Check for replenishment exactly once, at the end of round 1: if you hold fewer than two cards, take B2. Otherwise it stays in the reserve, with no later opportunity to take it. After round 3, add your points; unused cards score nothing. Aim for the highest total. Plans with equal totals have equal results.
The same 2 points leave different options
First, use the specialist card:
Time · Choice and points · Hand afterward
Round 1 · Play B1 for the blue job: 2 points. Take B2 afterward. · W, B2
Round 2 · Play B2 for the blue job: 4 points. · W
Round 3 · Play W for the red job: 3 points. · Empty

The total is 9, with all three cards discarded. Compare another legal sequence: play W in round 1 for 2 points, leaving B1 and B2 after replenishment; play B1 in round 2 for 4; then pass in round 3 because B2 cannot handle red. The total is 6. W and B1 are discarded, while B2 remains in hand.

The immediate reward for either first play is identical. The score difference appears in round 3: spending W also spends the only tool that can handle red. Keeping a card does not necessarily preserve an equally useful option. Holding B2 at the end still gives you no legal play for that job.

Here, hand management means arranging the use, retention, and replenishment of available cards to connect present actions with later ones. It concerns when a card becomes available, where it goes after use, and what the cards you keep can do.
Move only the replenishment check
Restart with one change: move the single replenishment check from the end of round 1 to the end of round 2. Keep all cards, jobs, points, and the hand limit unchanged.

If you still play B1 for 2 points in round 1, you start round 2 holding only W. Completing that blue job for 4 points requires spending W. You then receive B2, which cannot handle the final red job. Total: 6. Passing in round 2 to keep W for red instead gives 2 + 0 + 3 = 5.

A better sequence is to pass in round 1, play B1 for 4 points in round 2, take B2, and play W for 3 in round 3. You finish with 7 points and B2 in hand. Forgoing the smaller immediate reward preserves the combination needed for the later jobs.

Seven is the maximum in this version. Scoring the red job requires keeping W. Before B2 arrives, B1 can complete only one of the two blue jobs, so choose the 4-point job. Using W for blue instead allows at most 6 points from the two blue jobs.
Both versions contain exactly three cards. Their availability changes the result. B2 is visibly on the table, but it cannot help before it enters your hand.
Distinguish the related ideas

There is no shuffle or random draw here, yet there is hand management. Nor does play change the composition of a cycling deck, so this is not a demonstration of deck building. W's two uses make the cost of keeping it clearer. Cards with a single use can also create retention decisions when their uses and useful moments differ.

Acquiring more cards is different from using them well. Two blue cards are both unsuitable for red. A hand limit says how many cards you may keep, not which ones to keep. A design must also specify how many cards arrive, when the limit is checked, and what happens if it is exceeded.

This example reveals the future, allowing us to calculate a maximum. With hidden future jobs, players must choose using the information available at the time; hindsight alone cannot establish that an earlier decision was poor. Retention may also matter less if cards can always be exchanged freely for each other or immediately recovered after use.
Self-check: does playing nothing let you save more?
In the original version, suppose you pass in round 1, then play B1 in round 2 and W in round 3. Where is B2 at the end, and what is your total?

B2 remains in the reserve. B1 and W fill your two-card hand when the single replenishment check occurs, so B2 cannot enter. The later jobs award 4 and 3 points, totaling 7. Both starting cards end in the discard area. Keeping every card can also mean missing a replenishment opportunity.

For your own design, examine one decision: what future use did the player surrender? Which job expires before the next card arrives? If someone reports having cards but being unable to act, inspect card functions, arrival times, and action conditions before deciding whether to change card quantities or the rules for moving them.
References and classification

Geoffrey Engelstein and Isaac Shalev, Building Blocks of Tabletop Game Design: An Encyclopedia of Mechanisms, Second Edition, CRC Press, 2022: CAR-04, “Card Draw, Limits, and Deck Exhaustion”; CAR-08, “Multi-Use Cards.” Publication information

轮抽：我拿走这一张，谁的选择变了？
公开摆着两张相同的月亮卡，为什么有人愿意先拿一张，有人却想先拿太阳？因为同一张牌，对不同玩家未必有同样价值。拿牌又会改变别人接下来能选什么。轮抽的判断就发生在自己的需要与逐渐减少的机会之间。
三个人分六张卡
下面是自行构造的局部游戏。A、B、C 三人分配六张公开图案卡：太阳 1、太阳 2，月亮 1、月亮 2，星星 1、星星 2。编号只用于区分同图案的两张牌，不影响分数。每位玩家的计分表都公开：
谁拿到这张卡 · 每张太阳 · 每张月亮 · 每张星星
A · 3 分 · 2 分 · 0 分
B · 0 分 · 3 分 · 2 分
C · 1 分 · 4 分 · 0 分
按 A、B、C、A、B、C 的顺序，每人每次必须从公共区拿一张，免费、正面朝上放到自己面前。拿走的牌不补充，其他人不能再拿；不允许跳过、交换或弃牌，也没有另一个买牌阶段。两张同图案可以都拿，分别计分。
第六次取选后，每人恰有两张牌，公共区为空，立即结束。每人把自己两张的分数相加，最高者获胜，最高分并列则共享胜利。没有隐藏牌，也没有秘密目标。
走完一次取选，看机会如何减少
为了比较过程，先让三人采用同一种简单选法：每次都拿当前对自己分数最高的牌，同图案优先拿编号小的。这只是这里采用的选择方法，不是规则强迫玩家这样做，也不保证长远最好。
次数 · 玩家拿牌 · 公共区剩余数量：太阳／月亮／星星
6 · C 只能拿星星 2，值 0 分 · 0／0／0
A 共 6 分，B 共 5 分，C 共 4 分，A 获胜。六张牌全部转移到三人面前，没有牌被复制或消失。
注意第三次取选。月亮对 C 值 4 分，对 B 值 3 分；C 取走最后一张月亮后，B 第二次取选的最好选择只剩星星。C 得到的分数与 B 失去的机会，是同一次取选的两个后果。即使 C 只想着自己拿 4 分，也会产生这个影响。
轮抽是按规定的取选过程，把牌或其他游戏要素分配给玩家。这里演示的是公开轮抽：选择池可见，取走一张就从公共机会中移除一张。它比“拿到一张牌”多了两个关系：玩家能从哪些选项中挑，以及哪些人会在自己下一次取选前改变这些选项。
只把第二轮的次序倒过来
重开同样的六张牌，只把取选顺序改为 A、B、C、C、B、A，常称为蛇形顺序。计分表和刚才的选法都不变。
前三次仍是 A 拿太阳 1，B 拿月亮 1，C 拿月亮 2。此时剩太阳 2、星星 1、星星 2。第四次改由 C 拿太阳 2，值 1 分；第五次 B 拿星星 1，值 2 分；最后 A 只能拿星星 2，值 0 分。
结果变成 A 3 分、B 5 分、C 5 分，B 与 C 共享胜利。A 的第一次取选没有变，第二次却晚了：原本能拿到的太阳已被 C 取走。C 第一次在三人中最后选，现在换得连续两次取选。
倒序把两次取选的位置重新搭配，并不自动保证公平。这里三人的计分需求本就不同，也只比较了一种选法；不能凭一次分配判断哪个顺序普遍更好。设计师需要看牌的相对价值，以及重要的组合是否会在某个位置之前被拿光。
公开挑选、传递手牌与截走机会
轮抽也可以采用传递手牌的形式：各人从收到的一组牌中留下牌，把未选的部分传给下一人。大家可以同时作决定，但每个人通常只面对自己收到的那部分选项，某张牌可能在到自己手中以前就被拿走。它与全桌面对同一个公开池，在信息和可接触的选项上有区别。
随机发一张、没有选择，不是在演示这里的轮抽关系；从自己早已拥有的手牌中决定先用哪张，则主要是手牌使用问题。轮抽负责分配机会，取得的牌何时能用、是否还要付使用费，需要另外规定。本例直接留牌计分，因此没有后一笔费用。
玩家有时会拿走自己不太需要、别人很需要的牌。这是轮抽可能产生的一种选择行为，不是每次都应执行的额外规则。它可能牺牲自己的收益，也需要知道或推测别人的需要。公开池越大、计分组合越多，比较的工作也可能越多；最后只剩一张时，有取牌动作，却已没有图案可选。
自查：截走太阳，会让 C 更好吗？
回到原顺序 A、B、C、A、B、C。前两次不变，第三次 C 改拿太阳 2；之后三人继续按“当前对自己分数最高”取选。结果怎样？
剩下月亮 2 和两张星星。A 第四次拿月亮 2，B 第五次拿星星 1，C 最后拿星星 2。总分为 A：3＋2＝5；B：3＋2＝5；C：1＋0＝1。A 和 B 共享胜利。
C 确实让 A 比原过程少了 1 分，但自己从 4 分降到 1 分。截走别人所需，不等于改善自己的结果。回到自己的设计，可以记录：玩家预测会留下哪张牌？在下一次轮到他之前，谁需要它？如果总有一种牌无人愿取，先查它对不同玩家何时有用，以及拿它会放弃什么，而不是只看它有没有漂亮的牌面。
参考与分类检索
